name: MongoDB Atlas
summary: Managed MongoDB document database with built-in full-text search, vector search and change streams.
use_cases: Apps with evolving, nested data; products that need search and semantic/vector retrieval next to operational data; event-driven features via change streams.
tradeoffs: Requires a MongoDB Atlas cloud account; Atlas itself cannot be self-hosted.
Heavily relational data with many joins needs careful schema design in a document model.
avoid_if: you must self-host every component or your data is fundamentally relational with many cross-entity joins.

name: MongoDB Community Edition
summary: Self-managed MongoDB server; search and vector search are available via the mongot process.
use_cases: Teams that want the MongoDB document model on their own infrastructure, on-premises deployments, local development.
tradeoffs: You operate backups, upgrades, replication and the separate search process yourself.
SSPL is source-available but not OSI-approved, which matters for some open-source policies.
avoid_if: your organisation requires an OSI-approved licence or you have no capacity to run database operations.

name: PostgreSQL
summary: Mature open-source relational database with strong SQL, transactions and a large extension ecosystem (e.g. pgvector).
use_cases: Transactional business data, relational schemas, reporting, apps that want one well-understood database; vector search via the pgvector extension.
tradeoffs: Self-hosting means owning backups, failover and upgrades; managed offerings vary by provider.
Vector search relies on the pgvector extension rather than being built in.
avoid_if: you need built-in realtime sync to clients or offline-first mobile sync without extra tooling.

name: Supabase
summary: Open-source Postgres development platform bundling auth, realtime subscriptions, storage and edge functions.
use_cases: Small teams wanting a Firebase-style backend on top of Postgres; CRUD apps with auth and realtime updates; prototypes that may later self-host.
tradeoffs: Self-hosting runs several services (via Docker) and is noticeably more work than the managed platform.
Realtime is change broadcast, not an offline-first sync engine.
avoid_if: you need offline-first clients with automatic conflict resolution.

name: Firebase (Cloud Firestore)
summary: Google's managed app platform; Firestore is a document database with realtime listeners and offline persistence in client SDKs.
use_cases: Mobile and web apps that need realtime updates and offline support quickly, with auth and hosting from the same vendor.
tradeoffs: Strong coupling to Google Cloud; migrating away later is costly.
Query model is more limited than SQL (e.g. joins and some aggregations).
avoid_if: you must self-host or want to avoid vendor lock-in.

name: Redis
summary: In-memory data store used for caching, sessions, pub/sub, streams and (in Redis 8) query and vector search.
use_cases: Caching, rate limiting, session storage, leaderboards, lightweight pub/sub and job queues (e.g. via BullMQ).
tradeoffs: Data lives in memory, so large datasets get expensive.
Licensing changed in 2024 and again in 2025; check that the AGPL option fits your policy.
avoid_if: you need it as the primary system of record for large, durable datasets.

name: SQLite
summary: Embedded, serverless SQL database engine stored in a single file.
use_cases: Local-first and offline apps, mobile/desktop storage, tests, small to medium single-server web apps.
tradeoffs: One writer at a time; not designed for high write concurrency across many clients.
No built-in network server or replication.
avoid_if: many application servers must write to the same database concurrently.

name: Neon
summary: Serverless Postgres with separated storage and compute, scale-to-zero and database branching.
use_cases: Postgres for serverless apps, preview environments per branch, spiky or low-traffic workloads.
licence: Apache-2.0 (engine); typically used as a managed service
tradeoffs: Cold starts after scale-to-zero add latency to the first query.
Self-hosting the Neon engine is possible but not a typical path.
avoid_if: you need a self-hosted database with a well-trodden operations story.

name: Apache CouchDB
summary: Document database built around an HTTP API and a multi-master replication protocol.
use_cases: Offline-first apps that sync with PouchDB clients, multi-site replication, simple HTTP/JSON storage.
tradeoffs: Conflicts are detected but resolution logic is up to the application.
Smaller ecosystem and managed-hosting options than mainstream databases.
avoid_if: you need rich ad-hoc querying or a large managed-service ecosystem.

name: PouchDB
summary: JavaScript database that runs in the browser or Node and syncs with CouchDB-compatible servers.
use_cases: Offline-first web apps that store data locally and sync when online.
tradeoffs: Needs a CouchDB-compatible server for sync.
Slower release cadence than newer local-first tools.
avoid_if: you want real-time collaborative text editing (a CRDT library is a better fit).
